name: Wyoming

bills.title: Protecting kids from deepfakes and exploitative images.
Ban on government social scoring with AI.
Biometric data and license plate readers-regulation.

context:
Wyoming's 2026 budget session produced exactly one artificial intelligence law and killed two others, and the contrast tells you more about the state's posture than the single enactment does on its own. House Bill 102, titled protecting kids from deepfakes and exploitative images, was signed by the governor on 7 March 2026. It creates criminal offenses reaching synthetic sexual material depicting minors and AI generated deepfakes, and it passed with almost no dissent, clearing the House 58 to 1 and the Senate 31 to 0. Wyoming budget sessions are short and require a two thirds vote simply to introduce a bill that is not a budget measure, so a policy bill getting through at all signals unusual consensus.

The two bills that failed were the structurally ambitious ones. House Bill 91 would have barred government entities from using artificial intelligence to assign social scores to people or to identify them through biometric data and image gathering, subject to stated exceptions. It cleared committee and then died on 23 February 2026 when the House Committee of the Whole did not take it up for debate. House Bill 181 went further, proposing to prohibit governmental use of biometric identification systems, geolocation tracking and automatic license plate readers, and to restrict contracts with third party vendors supplying them. It never survived the introduction stage, failing on 13 February 2026. Both had bipartisan sponsorship. The pattern is that Wyoming legislators moved quickly on artificial intelligence used to harm children and not at all on artificial intelligence used by their own government.

One bill in this site's tracked list for Wyoming does not belong there, and it is worth saying so plainly. Senate File 22, amendments to the unincorporated nonprofit associations statutes, was signed on 3 March 2026. It concerns conversion procedures and wind down asset distribution for decentralized and standard unincorporated nonprofit associations, and it has nothing to do with artificial intelligence. It is a keyword false positive, and a reader counting Wyoming's AI enactments should count one, not two.

The more important point is that Wyoming has no comprehensive consumer data privacy statute and no general artificial intelligence act, yet AI conduct in the state is not unregulated. The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act, at Title 40 Chapter 12 of the Wyoming Statutes, prohibits misrepresentations and unfair or deceptive acts and practices in consumer transactions for personal, family or household purposes. That language does not mention artificial intelligence and does not need to. A company that overstates what its AI product can do, that misrepresents whether a customer is talking to a person or a machine, or that markets an automated service on false claims is exposed under the same provision that reaches any other deceptive sales practice. The Attorney General's Consumer Protection and Antitrust Unit may investigate and sue in the name of the state whenever it has reasonable cause to believe the Act has been violated and that proceedings serve the public interest.

As of early September 2026 there is no published Wyoming Attorney General guidance specific to artificial intelligence, no announced AI investigation, and no AI enforcement action on the office's public record. That absence is a finding rather than a gap in this summary. Wyoming's AI exposure today runs through general consumer protection law and one narrow criminal statute, and nothing else.

reading.body:
Wyoming has four active AI-related bills as of September 2026, focused on child protection, government surveillance, and biometric data rather than compute infrastructure or power.

The bills cluster around surveillance and harms prevention. HB0091 bans government social scoring with AI. HB0181 regulates biometric data and license plate readers. HB0102 targets deepfakes and exploitative images of children. SF0022 amends nonprofit association rules, with unclear direct AI connection from the title alone. None address data centers, power consumption, grid capacity, or compute availability.

This reflects a pattern in state AI regulation: lawmakers tackle visible harms and civil liberties before infrastructure. Wyoming's bills do not cover the physical constraints on AI scaling. They also do not distinguish between AI capabilities or acknowledge that constraint on compute may matter more to state policy than regulation of existing AI use.
